To perorate means to speak at great length in a grand, formal, or pompous way — often to the point where the listener feels the speaker is going on far too long and enjoying the sound of their own voice a little too much.

Think of a politician who, instead of making a simple point, launches into a sweeping, dramatic, elaborate speech that stretches on and on — full of lofty language, big gestures, and soaring declarations. That politician is perorating.

This word carries two distinct but related meanings, and understanding both is important.

Meaning 1 — The more common, everyday use:
To speak at tedious, excessive, or pompous length. The tone here is slightly critical. When you say someone "perorated," you are gently (or not so gently) mocking them for overdoing it — for being long-winded and self-important in their speech.

The professor perorated for forty minutes about a topic that needed only five.

She perorated endlessly at dinner, lecturing everyone about a subject no one had asked about.

Meaning 2 — The formal, rhetorical use:
To deliver the conclusion of a formal speech — the closing, wrapping-up section where the speaker pulls everything together and ends with force. This is a technical sense borrowed from classical public speaking.

The senator perorated with a passionate call to action that brought the crowd to its feet.

In this sense, it does not carry the mocking tone — it simply means the speaker is delivering their grand finale.

The meaning you take from "perorate" often depends on who is saying it and how.

  • If a critic says a speaker "perorated," they almost certainly mean the speaker droned on pompously and self-indulgently.
  • If a speechwriter or debate coach says a speaker "perorated well," they likely mean the speaker delivered a powerful, well-crafted closing.

In modern everyday writing and conversation, Meaning 1 (long-winded and pompous) is far more common. When in doubt, that is the safe assumption.

"Perorate" has a formal, slightly elevated register — meaning you will encounter it more in essays, literary criticism, political commentary, and sophisticated journalism than in casual conversation. It is the kind of word a writer reaches for when they want to describe a speaker with a hint of dry wit or disapproval.

It also implies a performance quality — someone who perorates is not just talking; they are holding forth, as if on a stage, aware of an audience, relishing the spotlight.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Ramble — to talk in a disorganized, wandering way. Rambling is messy. Perorating is grand and deliberate — it thinks it is impressive.
  • Lecture — to speak instructively, often in a one-sided way. Lecturing implies authority. Perorating implies showiness.
  • Orate — to make a formal speech. Neutral or positive in tone. Perorating is like orating but taken too far, or with excessive drama at the close.
  • Pontificate — the closest cousin. Both words describe pompous, self-important speech. "Pontificate" suggests someone speaking as if they are the ultimate authority. "Perorate" focuses more on the length, grandness, and theatrical quality of the speech.

One Final Example to Tie It Together

Imagine a CEO addressing employees after a merger. A simple, direct CEO would say: "This merger will open new opportunities for all of us. Thank you." But a CEO who perorates would spend forty-five minutes weaving a grand narrative about the arc of history, the courage of visionaries, the destiny of the company — with dramatic pauses, soaring language, and a thunderous closing — leaving everyone exhausted and slightly bewildered.

That, in a nutshell, is what it means to perorate.
